'Parth, why are you still awake?' Sabina asked from the doorway.

'Chemistry, maths, the physics file, the project, the library book...' Parth's voice cracked. 'Mummy, it's all in my head at once.'

'Then get it out of your head.' She put a notebook and pen in front of him. 'Write everything. Don't sort yet.'

Parth wrote for five minutes. Eleven lines. He stared at them. 'That's all?'

'That's all,' said Sabina. 'Now circle what has to happen tomorrow.'

He circled three. 'Chemistry chapter, the maths sheet and the file.'

'And the rest?'

'Later. The book goes back on Saturday.' He let out a long breath. 'It looks smaller on paper.'

'Sleep. The list will still be there in the morning.'

How was Parth feeling when he could not sleep?
qa.a: Parth felt overwhelmed and worried, since everything was in his head at once.

qa.q: What else could Parth do the next morning with the list?
qa.a: Parth could put a time beside each item for today, or tick items off as they get done, so the list turns into a plan.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel watching Parth work through the list?
qa.a: Sabina may feel concerned at first and then relieved to see Parth calmer and ready to sleep.

grounding: Shows a student writing all tasks down, feeling less worried, and sorting them into today and later.

passage:
I'm Chaitanya, and three weeks before my Class 10 prelims I couldn't sleep. My head felt like a browser with fifty tabs open. Maths revision. The science project. Return the library book. Hindi essay. Practical file. Pay the bus fee. It all kept spinning.
My older cousin Yogesh saw me lying awake at midnight and handed me a notebook. "Write everything down. Everything. Don't sort it yet."
I wrote for ten minutes. Twenty-three things. Seeing them on paper, they suddenly looked smaller. Just a list.
Then Yogesh said, "Now make two columns. Today. Later."
Today got four things: finish the practical file, return the book, one maths chapter, ask Papa about the bus fee. Everything else went to Later.
I slept that night. First time in a week.

qa.q: How many things did Chaitanya write down?
How did Chaitanya feel after seeing the list on paper?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt calmer and relieved, since the tasks suddenly looked smaller once they were written down.

qa.q: What else could Chaitanya do with the Later column?
qa.a: Chaitanya could move three or four items into Today each evening, so the Later list keeps shrinking.

qa.q: How might Yogesh see Chaitanya sleeping that night?
qa.a: Yogesh would likely feel glad and relieved that the simple list helped a worried cousin rest.

grounding: It shows a student with many tasks before exams writing them all down, which lowers worry and lets the tasks be sorted into today and later.

passage:
School counsellor's note, 3 February
Sachin, Class 12, came in today. He said he couldn't focus on anything because he kept remembering things he hadn't done. He was rubbing his forehead the whole time.
I didn't give advice at first. I gave him a sheet of paper and asked him to write down every task on his mind, big or small, without sorting.
He wrote for about eight minutes: board practicals, physics revision, college forms, a friend's birthday gift, fixing his cycle, and more. Seventeen items.
When he looked at the page, his shoulders dropped. He said, "It's less than it felt like."
Then he drew a line and sorted: today, this week, after exams. Today had three things.
He took the sheet with him. I will check in with him next Monday about how the week went.
— Pema, counsellor

qa.q: How many items did Sachin write?
What does Sachin's shoulders dropping suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt relieved and less overwhelmed once the tasks were on paper and looked smaller.

qa.q: What else could Sachin do each morning with the list?
qa.a: He could pick the top three from this week's column, so he always knows what comes next without holding it all in his head.

qa.q: How might Pema see the session?
qa.a: Pema sees that writing the list helped Sachin calm down quickly, and plans to check in next Monday.

grounding: It shows a student with many tasks writing them all down, which lowers his worry and lets him sort them into today and later.
